page.after:
What the differences mean

Four figures decide whether a battery runs a 240 V well pump.

  • Starting load. A submersible motor draws its locked-rotor current for a moment every time it starts. Franklin's 230 V 4-inch figures, as quoted by offgridbenchmark: 1/2 HP 3-wire 23 A × 230 V = 5,290 VA; 1/2 HP 2-wire 32.2 A × 230 V = 7,406 VA; 3/4 HP 3-wire 34.2 A × 230 V = 7,866 VA.
  • What the F3800 Plus can give. Anker rates the L14-30R at 25 A: 25 A × 240 V = 6,000 W. Anker publishes no surge figure. Zelpio measured about 7,200 W before shutoff but did not say what the load was. 5,290 VA is below both figures; 7,406 VA and 7,866 VA are above 7,200 W. Plan this kit for a 1/2 HP 3-wire pump.
  • How long one battery lasts. Zelpio measured about 112 W of idle draw: 112 W × 24 h = 2,688 Wh a day, which is 70% of the 3,840 Wh battery before the pump runs at all. The pump itself: 300 gal a day (the EPA's figure for an average family) ÷ 10 gal/min (offgridbenchmark's flow assumption) = 30 min × 960 W = 480 Wh. 3,840 Wh ÷ 3,168 Wh a day ≈ 1.2 days.
  • Refill time. Through the bypass cable, a 240 V generator recharges the F3800 Plus at up to 3,300 W (Anker): 3,840 Wh ÷ 3,300 W ≈ 1.2 h of generator time, before charging losses.
Your pump and outageWhat fits
1/2 HP 3-wire 240 V pump, and you own a 240 V (L14-30) generatorThe Anker kit below. Run the generator about an hour and a quarter a day.
1/2 HP 3-wire, smaller budget, short outagesOSCAL PowerMax 6000 (7,200 W surge rated, 120/240 V from one unit) or 2× Growatt HELIOS 3600 + hub
1/2 HP 2-wire, or 3/4 HP and upNone of the stations above publishes a start figure of 7,406 VA or more. Anker's well-pump guide rates its E10 system at up to 120 A locked-rotor with one E10 and one battery module. The other route is a 240 V gas generator sized to the pump's starting watts.

The recharge trap: 240 V stops while charging on 120 V

Anker's F3800 Plus page says: “The 240V output cannot be used while the device is charging via 120V AC.” A well pump on the L14-30R outlet loses power as soon as the station is topped up from a wall outlet or from a 120 V generator. With only 120 V wall charging connected, Anker's bundle listing shows the TT-30R (1,440 W bypass) and three 5-20R outlets live and the L14-30R off.

Anker's 240V Bypass Charging Cable, which its FAQ calls the Generator Input Adapter, solves this. It takes a 240 V generator's L14-30 output, and Anker says “your generator can charge F3800 Plus while supplying power to the load.” It accepts up to 6,000 W at 240 V and recharges at 3,300 W. While it is connected, the 5-20R outlets are disabled. It needs an L1+L2+N+PE 60 Hz system and must never be connected to the grid.

The kit: {kit:kit-well-pump-240v-battery-backup} the F3800 Plus + Smart Home Power Kit (Smart Home Panel, subpanel, breaker and ground bar; Anker says the panel supports 120/240 V split-phase systems only) and the 240V Bypass Charging Cable. Both come from one Anker cart for $4,799.99 + $399.99 = $5,199.98 on 2026-11-10. The pump's 2-pole breaker should match the pump nameplate. For outages longer than about a day, add Anker's BP3800 battery (3,840 Wh).

Not recommended: one Growatt HELIOS 3600 for a 240 V pump

Growatt's listing says the HELIOS 3600 supports “240V whole-home power when parallel two HELIOS 3600s.” One unit's high-current outlets are a TT-30 and a 30 A Anderson. A 240 V pump needs two units plus the Double Voltage Power Hub (two L14-30, one 6-20, 7,200 W combined): 2 × $1,198.98 + $139 = $2,536.96 on 2026-11-10. Growatt gives 7,200 W as combined output, not as a surge rating.
